html:
A network of buried pipes that carries water from wells deep under the Sahara to the cities on Libya's Mediterranean coast. Work began in 1984. It is the largest irrigation project in the world.

Under the desert lies the Nubian Sandstone Aquifer System, a vast store of fossil water that soaked in thousands of years ago, when the Sahara was green. It is barely refilled today. Hundreds of wells pump it into pipes four metres across, which carry it hundreds of kilometres north to Tripoli, Benghazi and other towns.

Muammar Gaddafi called it the eighth wonder of the world and paid for it with oil money. The first water reached Benghazi in 1991. It supplies most of the drinking water of Libya's cities and lets farms grow food in the desert.

Its critics say the water is being mined and will run out, and that much of it was used to grow crops that could be bought more cheaply abroad. Since the civil wars that followed Gaddafi's fall in 2011, attacks, theft and lack of repair have damaged the system.
sum: A network of buried pipes that carries water from wells deep under the Sahara to the cities on Libya's Mediterranean coast. Work began in 1984. It is the largest irrigation project in the world.
